chapters.title: Units and Measurements
points: SI system has 7 base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), candela (luminous intensity), mole (amount of substance).
Significant figures: all certain digits plus the first uncertain digit. In multiplication/division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the quantity with the least.
Errors: absolute error = |measured value - true value|; relative error = absolute error / true value; percentage error = relative error x 100.
Dimensions express a quantity in terms of [M], [L], [T] etc. Example: force = [M L T^-2], energy = [M L^2 T^-2], pressure = [M L^-1 T^-2].
Dimensional analysis checks an equation's consistency and converts units, but it cannot find dimensionless constants like 1/2 or 2pi.
Least count: vernier callipers LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD (commonly 0.01 cm); screw gauge LC = pitch / number of circular scale divisions (commonly 0.001 cm).
Parallax method measures large distances: D = b / theta, where b is the baseline and theta the parallax angle in radians.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The volume of a cube of side 1 cm is equal to _____ m^3.
The number of significant figures in 0.06900 is: (a) 5 (b) 4 (c) 2 (d) 3
questions.a: (b) 4. The zeros to the left of the first non-zero digit are not counted, but the trailing zeros are significant.

questions.q: The period of oscillation of a simple pendulum is assumed to depend on the length l and the acceleration due to gravity g. Derive the form of the period T by the method of dimensions.
questions.a: T = k x sqrt(l/g), where k is a dimensionless constant (actually 2pi). T is proportional to l^(1/2) g^(-1/2).

questions.q: Convert 1 kg m^2 s^-2 into g cm^2 s^-2.

chapters.title: Motion in a Straight Line
points: Displacement is the shortest straight-line change in position (a vector); distance is the total path length (a scalar). Displacement can be zero or negative, distance cannot.
Average velocity = displacement / time; instantaneous velocity v = dx/dt. Average speed = total distance / total time.
Acceleration a = dv/dt; the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement; the slope of a position-time graph gives velocity.
Equations of uniformly accelerated motion: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
Distance covered in the nth second: s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1).
For free fall under gravity, a = g = 9.8 m/s^2 downward; a body thrown up reaches max height h = u^2/(2g) in time t = u/g.
Relative velocity of A w. B is v_AB = v_A - v_B (in one dimension with signs).

questions.q: Can the following be treated as point objects: (a) a railway carriage moving smoothly between two stations, (b) a spinning cricket ball that turns sharply on hitting the ground? Give reasons.
questions.a: (a) Yes - the size of the carriage is negligible compared with the distance between stations. (b) No - the ball's size is comparable with the distance over which it changes direction, and its spin matters.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a velocity of 20 m/s from the top of a building 25 m above the ground. (a) How high does the ball rise above the ground? (b) How long before it hits the ground? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
questions.a: (a) It rises u^2/(2g) = 400/19.6 = 20.4 m above the top, i.e. 45.4 m above the ground. (b) Solving 25 = -20t + 4.9t^2 gives t = about 5.1 s.

questions.q: A particle moves with x(t) = x0(1 - e^-gt), t >= 0, x0 > 0. Where does it start, and with what velocity?
questions.a: At t = 0, x = x0(1 - 1) = 0. Velocity v = dx/dt = x0 g e^-gt, so v(0) = x0 g. It starts at the origin with speed x0 g.

questions.q: A particle in one-dimensional motion has zero speed at an instant. Can it have non-zero acceleration at that instant? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes. A ball thrown vertically upward has zero velocity at its highest point, but the acceleration there is still g downward.

chapters.title: Motion in a Plane
points: A vector has magnitude and direction. Resultant of two vectors: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta); direction tan phi = B sin theta / (A + B cos theta).
Dot product A. B = AB cos theta (scalar, used for work); cross product |A x B| = AB sin theta (vector, used for torque), direction by right-hand rule.
Projectile motion: time of flight T = 2u sin theta / g; max height H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2g); range R = u^2 sin 2theta / g. Range is maximum at theta = 45 degrees.
Uniform circular motion: centripetal acceleration a = v^2/r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre; period T = 2pi/omega.
For a projectile, horizontal velocity stays constant (no horizontal acceleration) while vertical velocity changes under gravity.
Unit vectors i, j, k have magnitude 1 along x, y, z axes; any vector A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k with |A| = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2).

questions.q: State which of the following are scalars and which are vectors: volume, speed, density, acceleration, velocity, angular velocity.
questions.a: Scalars: volume, speed, density. Vectors: acceleration, velocity, displacement, angular velocity.

questions.q: A cyclist rides at 27 km/h and, approaching a circular turn of radius 80 m, brakes, reducing his speed at 0.50 m/s^2. Find the magnitude and direction of the net acceleration on the turn.
questions.a: v = 7.5 m/s. Centripetal acceleration = v^2/r = 0.70 m/s^2. Net acceleration = sqrt(0.70^2 + 0.50^2) = 0.86 m/s^2 at an angle tan^-1(0.7/0.5) = about 54.5 deg to the direction of velocity.

questions.q: 'The net acceleration of a particle in circular motion is always along the radius towards the centre.' True or false? Give a reason.
questions.a: False. It is true only for uniform circular motion. If the speed changes there is also a tangential component of acceleration.

questions.q: A fighter plane flies horizontally at 1.5 km altitude with speed 720 km/h, passing over an anti-aircraft gun. At what angle from the vertical should the gun (muzzle speed 600 m/s) be fired to hit the plane, and above what altitude would the plane be safe?
questions.a: (a) The shell must have the plane's horizontal speed: sin(theta) = 200/600, so theta = about 19.5 deg from the vertical. (b) The plane must fly higher than the shell's maximum height, about 16 km.

chapters.title: Laws of Motion
points: Newton's first law: a body resists change in its state of rest or uniform motion (law of inertia). Inertia increases with mass.
Newton's second law: F = dp/dt = ma. Momentum p = mv. Impulse = F x t = change in momentum.
Newton's third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other.
Conservation of linear momentum: in the absence of external force, total momentum of a system stays constant (used in collisions and recoil).
Friction: static friction is self-adjusting up to f_max = mu_s N; kinetic friction f_k = mu_k N, with mu_k < mu_s. Friction opposes relative motion or its tendency.
Centripetal force needed for circular motion: F = mv^2/r. On a banked road the safe speed without friction is v = sqrt(rg tan theta).
Weight in a lift: apparent weight increases when the lift accelerates up (R = m(g + a)) and decreases when it accelerates down (R = m(g - a)); in free fall the person feels weightless.

questions.q: Give the magnitude and direction of the net force acting on a stone of mass 0.1 kg just after it is dropped from a window.
questions.a: Only gravity acts: F = mg = 0.1 x 10 = 1 N vertically downward.

questions.q: A constant retarding force of 50 N is applied to a body of mass 20 kg moving initially with a speed of 15 m/s. How long does the body take to stop?
questions.a: Retardation a = F/m = 50/20 = 2.5 m/s^2. Time t = v/a = 15/2.5 = 6 s.

questions.q: A body of mass 5 kg is acted upon by two perpendicular forces 8 N and 6 N. Give the magnitude and direction of its acceleration.
questions.a: Net force = sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = 10 N, so acceleration = 10/5 = 2 m/s^2, at an angle tan^-1(6/8) = about 36.9 deg to the 8 N force.

questions.q: A shell of mass 0.020 kg is fired by a gun of mass 100 kg. If the muzzle speed of the shell is 80 m/s, what is the recoil speed of the gun?
questions.a: By momentum conservation: 100 x V = 0.020 x 80 = 1.6, so V = 1.6 x 10^-2 m/s in the opposite direction.

chapters.title: Work, Energy and Power
points: Work W = F. s = Fs cos theta. Work is a scalar; it is zero if force or displacement is zero or if they are perpendicular.
Work-energy theorem: net work done on a body = change in its kinetic energy, W = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2.
Kinetic energy K = (1/2)mv^2 = p^2/(2m). Doubling speed makes K four times.
Potential energy: gravitational U = mgh near Earth's surface; spring potential energy = (1/2)kx^2; spring force F = -kx (Hooke's law).
Conservative forces (gravity, spring) do work independent of path; for them mechanical energy (K + U) is conserved when no other force does work.
Power P = W/t = F. v. 1 horsepower = 746 W.
Collisions: in elastic collisions both momentum and KE are conserved; in perfectly inelastic collisions bodies stick together and KE loss is maximum (momentum still conserved).

questions.q: State carefully whether the following quantities are positive or negative: (a) work done by a man in lifting a bucket out of a well, (b) work done by gravity in that case, (c) work done by friction on a body sliding down an incline, (d) work done by the resistive force of air on a vibrating pendulum.
questions.a: (a) Positive (force and displacement both upward). (b) Negative (gravity acts downward, displacement upward). (c) Negative (friction opposes motion). (d) Negative (air resistance opposes the velocity).

questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg initially at rest moves under an applied horizontal force of 7 N on a table with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.1. In 10 s, compute (a) work done by the applied force, (b) work done by friction, (c) work done by the net force, (d) change in kinetic energy.
questions.a: Net acceleration = (7 - 0.1x2x9.8)/2 = 2.52 m/s^2; distance in 10 s = 126 m. (a) 7 x 126 = 882 J. (b) -1.96 x 126 = -247 J. (c) 882 - 247 = 635 J. (d) Change in KE = 635 J - verifying the work-energy theorem.

questions.q: A body is initially at rest and undergoes one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration. The power delivered to it at time t is proportional to: (i) t^1/2 (ii) t (iii) t^3/2 (iv) t^2
questions.a: (ii) t. Power P = F x v = (ma)(at) = ma^2 t, which is proportional to t.

questions.q: A body moves unidirectionally under the influence of a source of constant power. Its displacement in time t is proportional to: (i) t^1/2 (ii) t (iii) t^3/2 (iv) t^2
questions.a: (iii) t^3/2. Constant power gives v dv/dx = constant, leading to x proportional to t^3/2.

chapters.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
points: Centre of mass of two particles: x_cm = (m1x1 + m2x2)/(m1 + m2). External force moves the CM as if all mass were concentrated there: F_ext = M a_cm.
Torque tau = r x F, magnitude rF sin theta. Angular momentum L = r x p = I omega; tau = dL/dt.
Moment of inertia I = sum m_i r_i^2. Ring: MR^2; disc: (1/2)MR^2; solid sphere: (2/5)MR^2; rod about centre: ML^2/12 (all about central axes through CM).
Rotational KE = (1/2) I omega^2. Total KE of a rolling body = (1/2)Mv_cm^2 + (1/2)I_cm omega^2.
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md^2. Perpendicular axis theorem (for a plane lamina): I_z = I_x + I_y.
Angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is zero (e.g. a spinning skater speeds up by pulling arms in).
Rolling without slipping: v_cm = R omega, a_cm = R alpha. A solid sphere rolls down an incline faster than a ring because more of its energy is translational.

questions.q: Give the location of the centre of mass of (i) a sphere, (ii) a cylinder, (iii) a ring and (iv) a cube, each of uniform mass density. Does the centre of mass of a body necessarily lie inside the body?
questions.a: All four have their centre of mass at their geometric centre. No - e.g. the centre of mass of a ring lies at its centre, in empty space outside the material.

questions.q: A child sits stationary at one end of a long trolley moving uniformly with speed V on a smooth horizontal floor. If the child gets up and runs about on the trolley in any manner, what is the speed of the centre of mass of the (trolley + child) system?
questions.a: Still V. There is no net external horizontal force, so the velocity of the centre of mass of the system cannot change.

questions.q: A child stands at the centre of a turntable with arms outstretched, rotating at 40 rev/min. He folds his hands back, reducing his moment of inertia to 2/5 of its initial value. (a) What is his new angular speed? (b) Show that the new kinetic energy of rotation is more than the initial, and account for the increase.
questions.a: (a) By conservation of angular momentum: 40 x I = omega' x (2/5)I, so omega' = 100 rev/min. (b) KE scales as I x omega^2, so it becomes 2.5 times larger; the extra energy comes from the work done by the child's muscles in folding his arms.

questions.q: Why does a solid sphere have a smaller moment of inertia than a hollow cylinder of the same mass and radius, about an axis through their axes of symmetry?
questions.a: In the solid sphere the mass is distributed from the centre out to R, so the average r^2 is smaller; in the hollow cylinder all the mass is concentrated at distance R from the axis, giving a larger moment of inertia.

chapters.title: Gravitation
points: Newton's law of gravitation: F = G m1 m2 / r^2, with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. The force is always attractive.
Acceleration due to gravity: g = GM/R^2 at the surface. At height h: g' = g (R/(R+h))^2; at depth d: g' = g (1 - d/R). g decreases both ways.
Gravitational potential energy U = -GMm/r (zero at infinity). Potential V = -GM/r.
Orbital velocity of a satellite near Earth's surface v_o = sqrt(gR) = about 7.9 km/s. Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2) x v_o = about 11.2 km/s.
Kepler's laws: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus; areal velocity is constant; T^2 is proportional to r^3 (T^2/r^3 = constant).
A geostationary satellite has period 24 h, orbits in the equatorial plane at about 35,800 km height, and appears fixed in the sky.
Weightlessness in an orbiting satellite is due to free fall: satellite and everything inside fall towards Earth with the same acceleration g.

questions.q: Answer the following: (a) Can you shield a body from the gravitational influence of nearby matter by putting it inside a hollow sphere? (b) An astronaut in a small spaceship orbiting Earth cannot detect gravity. If the station were very large, could he detect gravity? (c) The Sun pulls Earth more strongly than the Moon does, yet the Moon's tidal effect is larger. Why?
questions.a: (a) No - gravity cannot be shielded by any material. (b) Yes - tidal (differential gravity) effects become detectable across a large station. (c) Tides depend on the difference of gravitational pull across Earth, which falls as 1/r^3; the Moon is much closer, so its tidal effect dominates.

questions.q: A rocket is fired from the Earth towards the Sun. At what distance from Earth's centre is the gravitational force on the rocket zero? (Mass of Sun = 2 x 10^30 kg, mass of Earth = 6 x 10^24 kg, Earth-Sun distance = 1.5 x 10^11 m.)
questions.a: At distance r from Earth: GMe/r^2 = GMs/(R - r)^2 gives (R - r)/r = sqrt(Ms/Me) = 577, so r = R/578 = about 2.6 x 10^8 m from Earth's centre.

questions.q: Both Earth and Moon are subject to the gravitational force of the Sun. As observed from the Sun, the orbit of the Moon: (a) will be elliptical, (b) will not be strictly elliptical because the total gravitational force on it is not central, (c) is not elliptical but will necessarily be a closed curve, (d) deviates considerably from being elliptical due to influence of other planets.
questions.a: (b) The total gravitational force on the Moon (Sun + Earth) is not central, so its orbit is not strictly elliptical.

questions.q: A Saturn year is 29.5 times the Earth year. How far is Saturn from the Sun if Earth is 1.50 x 10^8 km away from the Sun?
questions.a: By Kepler's third law: r_s = r_e x (29.5)^(2/3) = 1.50 x 10^8 x 9.55 = about 1.43 x 10^9 km.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
points: Stress = restoring force / area (N/m^2 or pascal). Strain = change in dimension / original dimension (no unit).
Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain. Young modulus Y = longitudinal stress / longitudinal strain = (F/A) / (delta L / L).
Bulk modulus B = -P / (delta V / V) (negative sign because volume decreases as pressure increases). Shear modulus G = shear stress / shear strain.
Poisson ratio = lateral strain / longitudinal strain (typically 0.2-0.4 for metals; theoretical limits -1 to 0.5).
The stress-strain curve: proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength, fracture point. Area under it gives energy stored per unit volume.
Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire = (1/2) x stress x strain x volume = (1/2) F x delta L.

questions.q: A steel wire of length 4.7 m and cross-sectional area 3.0 x 10^-5 m^2 stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length 3.5 m and area 4.0 x 10^-5 m^2 under the same load. What is the ratio of the Young's modulus of steel to that of copper?

The edge of an aluminium cube is 10 cm long. One face is fixed to a vertical wall and a mass of 100 kg is attached to the opposite face. The shear modulus of aluminium is 25 GPa. What is the vertical deflection of this face?
questions.a: Shear strain = F/(A x eta) = (100 x 10)/(0.01 x 25 x 10^9) = 4 x 10^-6. Deflection = strain x edge length = 4 x 10^-6 x 0.1 = 4 x 10^-7 m.

questions.q: Two identical steel cubes (mass 50 g, side 1 cm) collide head-on face to face, each with speed 10 cm/s. Find the maximum compression of each. (Young's modulus of steel Y = 2 x 10^11 N/m^2.)
questions.a: Initial KE = 2 x (1/2)mv^2 = 5 x 10^-4 J becomes elastic PE 2 x (1/2)K(delta L)^2 with K = YA/L = 2 x 10^11 x 0.01. Compression delta L = sqrt(5 x 10^-4/(2 x 10^11 x 0.1)) = about 1.58 x 10^-7 m.

questions.q: A copper piece with rectangular cross-section 15.2 mm x 19.1 mm is pulled in tension with a force of 44,500 N, producing only elastic deformation. Calculate the resulting strain. (Y_cu = 110 GPa.)

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
points: Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions (basis of the hydraulic lift: F2/F1 = A2/A1).
Pressure at depth h in a liquid: P = P_atm + rho g h. Pressure depends only on depth and density, not on the container's shape.
Archimedes' principle: upthrust = weight of liquid displaced = rho_liquid x V_submerged x g. A body floats when upthrust balances its weight.
Equation of continuity for incompressible flow: A1v1 = A2v2 - fluid speeds up in narrower sections.
Bernoulli's theorem (for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow): P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline.
Viscosity: Newton's law F = -eta A (dv/dx). Stokes' law for a sphere: F = 6 pi eta r v; terminal velocity v_t = 2r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta).
Surface tension S = F/l = energy per unit area. Excess pressure inside a liquid drop = 2S/R; inside a soap bubble = 4S/R. Capillary rise h = 2S cos theta / (rho g r).

questions.q: Streamline flow is more likely for liquids with: (a) high density (b) high viscosity (c) low density (d) low viscosity
questions.a: Both (b) and (c). High viscosity keeps the flow lines distinct, and low density keeps the Reynolds number (rvd/eta) low, both favouring streamline flow.

questions.q: Iceberg floats in water with part of it submerged. What fraction of the volume of the iceberg is submerged if the density of ice is 0.917 g/cm^3?
questions.a: Fraction submerged = density of ice / density of water = 0.917/1 = 0.917.

questions.q: Why is the blood pressure in humans greater at the feet than at the brain?
questions.a: Pressure in a fluid column is P = rho g h; the feet lie below the heart, so they carry the pressure of a taller column of blood than the brain does.

questions.q: A 50 kg girl wearing high heel shoes balances on a single heel. The heel is circular with diameter 1.0 cm. What is the pressure exerted by the heel on the horizontal floor?

chapters.title: Thermal Properties of Matter
points: Temperature scales: T(K) = t(deg C) + 273.15. Size of 1 degree is the same on Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Thermal expansion: linear delta L = alpha L delta T; area expansion coefficient beta = 2 alpha; volume expansion gamma = 3 alpha. For gases at constant pressure, gamma = 1/273 per degree C (ideal).
Specific heat capacity c: Q = m c delta T. Molar heat capacity uses moles. Water has a very high specific heat (4186 J/kg K), hence its use as a coolant.
Latent heat: Q = mL (no temperature change during phase change). Latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 x 10^5 J/kg; of vaporisation of water = 22.6 x 10^5 J/kg.
Heat transfer: conduction (Q/t = kA delta T / d), convection (fluid movement), radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann law P = sigma A T^4; Kirchhoff's law - good absorbers are good emitters).
Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling is proportional to the excess temperature of the body over surroundings (for small differences).
Wien's displacement law: lambda_max x T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K - hotter bodies radiate at shorter wavelengths.

questions.q: The triple points of neon and carbon dioxide are 24.57 K and 216.55 K respectively. Express these temperatures on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
questions.a: Neon: -248.58 deg C and -415.44 deg F. Carbon dioxide: -56.60 deg C and -69.88 deg F.

questions.q: Two absolute scales A and B have triple points of water defined to be 200 A and 350 B. What is the relation between T_A and T_B?

A brass wire 1.8 m long at 27 deg C is held taut with little tension between two rigid supports. If the wire is cooled to -39 deg C, what is the tension developed in the wire, if its diameter is 2.0 mm? (alpha_brass = 2.0 x 10^-5 per deg C, Y_brass = 0.91 x 10^11 Pa.)
questions.a: Thermal strain = alpha x delta T = 1.32 x 10^-3. Tension = Y x A x strain = 0.91 x 10^11 x pi x 10^-6 x 1.32 x 10^-3 = about 3.8 x 10^2 N.

questions.q: A body cools from 80 deg C to 50 deg C in 5 minutes. Calculate the time it takes to cool from 60 deg C to 30 deg C. The temperature of the surroundings is 20 deg C.
questions.a: By Newton's law of cooling, the rate constant K = (30/5)/(65 - 20) = 0.133 per min. Then (30/t) = K x (45 - 20), giving t = 9 minutes.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
points: Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other - this defines temperature.
First law: delta Q = delta U + delta W (heat supplied = increase in internal energy + work done BY the gas). Sign convention: work done by gas is positive.
Isothermal process (T constant): delta U = 0, W = nRT ln(V2/V1). Adiabatic process (Q = 0): PV^gamma = constant, W = (P1V1 - P2V2)/(gamma - 1).
Molar heat capacities: C_p - C_v = R; gamma = C_p/C_v = 1.67 (monoatomic), 1.4 (diatomic), 1.33 (triatomic non-linear approx).
Second law (Kelvin-Planck): no engine can convert all heat into work. Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T_cold/T_hot (temperatures in kelvin); it is the maximum possible.
Refrigerator COP = Q_cold / W = T_cold / (T_hot - T_cold) for a Carnot refrigerator.
Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature; for n moles of a gas with f degrees of freedom, U = (f/2) nRT.

questions.q: A geyser heats water flowing at the rate of 3.0 litres per minute from 27 deg C to 77 deg C. If the geyser operates on a gas burner, what is the rate of consumption of fuel if its heat of combustion is 4.0 x 10^4 J/g?
questions.a: Heat needed per minute = 3 x 4200 x 50 = 6.3 x 10^5 J. Fuel rate = 6.3 x 10^5/4.0 x 10^4 = about 16 g per minute.

questions.q: What amount of heat must be supplied to 2.0 x 10^-2 kg of nitrogen (at room temperature) to raise its temperature by 45 deg C at constant pressure? (Molecular mass of N2 = 28; R = 8.3 J/mol K.)
A refrigerator is to maintain eatables kept inside at 9 deg C. If the room temperature is 36 deg C, calculate the coefficient of performance.
A steam engine delivers 5.4 x 10^8 J of work per minute and services 3.6 x 10^9 J of heat per minute from its boiler. What is the efficiency of the engine? How much heat is wasted per minute?
questions.a: Efficiency = 5.4 x 10^8/3.6 x 10^9 = 0.15, i.e. 15%. Heat wasted = 3.6 x 10^9 - 5.4 x 10^8 = 3.06 x 10^9 J per minute.

chapters.title: Kinetic Theory
points: Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT = Nk_B T. Pressure from kinetic theory: P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2 = (2/3) x (KE per unit volume).
rms speed c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3k_B T/m). Average KE of one molecule = (3/2) k_B T; per mole = (3/2) RT.
Degrees of freedom: monoatomic gas f = 3 (translational); diatomic at room temperature f = 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). Equipartition: each degree of freedom carries (1/2) k_B T per molecule.
Law of equipartition links internal energy U = (f/2) nRT and heat capacities C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = (f/2 + 1) R.
Mean free path lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 N/V): increases when density decreases or molecule size decreases.
Maxwell speed distribution: most probable speed = sqrt(2RT/M), average speed = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)), rms speed = sqrt(3RT/M); rms is the largest of the three.

questions.q: Estimate the fraction of the molecular volume to the actual volume occupied by oxygen gas at STP. Take the diameter of an oxygen molecule to be 3 Angstrom.
questions.a: Molecular volume per mole = (4/3)pi(1.5 x 10^-10)^3 x N_A = about 8.5 x 10^-6 m^3. Molar volume at STP = 2.24 x 10^-2 m^3. Fraction = about 4 x 10^-4.

questions.q: At what temperature is the root mean square speed of an atom in an argon gas cylinder equal to the rms speed of a helium gas atom at -20 deg C? (Atomic mass of Ar = 39.9 u, of He = 4.0 u.)
questions.a: c_rms proportional to sqrt(T/M): T_Ar = 253 x (39.9/4.0) = about 2.52 x 10^3 K.

questions.q: A flask contains argon and chlorine in the ratio 2:1 by mass. The temperature of the mixture is 27 deg C. Obtain the ratio of (i) average kinetic energy per molecule, and (ii) root mean square speed of the molecules of the two gases. (Ar = 39.9 u, Cl2 = 70.9 u.)
questions.a: (i) 1:1 - average kinetic energy depends only on temperature. (ii) v_Ar/v_Cl = sqrt(70.9/39.9) = about 1.33.

questions.q: A cubic vessel (with faces horizontal and vertical) contains an ideal gas at NTP. The vessel is carried by a rocket moving at 500 m/s in the vertical direction. What is the pressure of the gas inside the vessel as observed from the ground?
questions.a: It remains the same. Motion of the vessel as a whole does not change the relative motion of the gas molecules with respect to the walls, which is what causes pressure.

chapters.title: Oscillations
points: SHM: displacement x = A sin(omega t + phi); acceleration a = -omega^2 x (always directed to mean position); velocity v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
Time period T = 2pi/omega; frequency nu = 1/T. For a spring-mass system T = 2pi sqrt(m/k); for a simple pendulum T = 2pi sqrt(l/g).
Energy in SHM: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2; total E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 stays constant (no friction).
KE and PE are equal at x = A/sqrt(2). At the mean position KE is maximum and PE minimum; at extremes the reverse.
Phase: two oscillators with phase difference 0 are in phase; pi means opposite phase. Phase difference = (2pi/lambda) x path difference in waves.

Damped oscillations lose amplitude gradually due to friction; forced oscillations take the driver's frequency; resonance occurs when driver frequency equals natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude.

questions.q: Which of the following represent periodic motion: (a) a swimmer completing one return trip from one bank of a river to the other and back, (b) a freely suspended bar magnet displaced from its N-S direction and released, (c) a hydrogen molecule rotating about its centre of mass, (d) an arrow released from a bow?
questions.a: (b) and (c). The magnet oscillates about its equilibrium direction and the molecule rotates periodically; the swimmer's trip and the arrow's flight are not repeated motions.

questions.q: Which of the following represent nearly SHM and which represent periodic but not SHM: (a) rotation of Earth about its axis, (b) motion of an oscillating mercury column in a U-tube, (c) motion of a ball bearing inside a smooth curved bowl released slightly above the lowest point, (d) general vibrations of a polyatomic molecule about its equilibrium position?
questions.a: Nearly SHM: (b) and (d) - the restoring force is nearly proportional to displacement. Periodic but not SHM: (a) and (c).

questions.q: A spring of force constant k is clamped rigidly at one end with a mass m at the free end; a force F stretches it. The same spring has both ends free with a mass m at each end, and each end is stretched by the same force F. (a) What is the maximum extension in the two cases? (b) If the mass(es) are released, what is the period of oscillation in each case?
questions.a: (a) F/k in both cases. (b) First case: T = 2pi sqrt(m/k). Second case: the reduced mass is m/2, so T = 2pi sqrt(m/2k).

questions.q: A spring balance has a scale that reads from 0 to 50 kg. The length of the scale is 20 cm. A body suspended from this balance, when displaced and released, oscillates with a period of 0.6 s. What is the weight of the body?
questions.a: k = (50 x 9.8)/0.2 = 2450 N/m. From T = 2pi sqrt(m/k): m = kT^2/4pi^2 = about 22.3 kg, so the weight is about 2.19 x 10^2 N.

chapters.title: Waves
points: Wave speed v = nu x lambda. Transverse waves (light, strings) vibrate perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate parallel, forming compressions and rarefactions.
Progressive wave equation: y = A sin(omega t - kx + phi), where k = 2pi/lambda is the propagation constant.
Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string v = sqrt(T/mu), where T is tension and mu is mass per unit length.
Speed of sound in a gas (Newton-Laplace): v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) = sqrt(gamma RT / M). Sound speed in air is about 332 m/s at 0 deg C and increases about 0.61 m/s per degree C rise.

Standing waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) form. String fixed at both ends: harmonics nu_n = n v/(2L), all harmonics present. Open organ pipe: all harmonics; closed pipe: only odd harmonics, fundamental nu = v/(4L).
Beats: when two sounds of close frequencies nu1 and nu2 play together, beat frequency = |nu1 - nu2|.
Doppler effect: apparent frequency changes when source and observer move relative to each other; frequency increases on approach, decreases on recession.

questions.q: You have learnt that a travelling wave in one dimension is represented by y = f(x +- vt). Is the converse true? Examine whether these can possibly represent a travelling wave: (a) (x - vt)^2, (b) log[(x + vt)/x0], (c) 1/(x + vt).
questions.a: Yes to all three. Any function of (x +- vt) keeps its shape while moving with speed v, so each can represent a travelling wave.

questions.q: A steel wire has a length of 12.0 m and a mass of 2.10 kg. What should be the tension in the wire so that the speed of a transverse wave on the wire equals the speed of sound in dry air at 20 deg C (343 m/s)?

A hospital uses an ultrasonic scanner to locate tumours in a tissue. What is the wavelength of sound in the tissue in which the speed of sound is 1.7 km/s? The operating frequency of the scanner is 4.2 MHz.
questions.a: lambda = v/f = 1700/4.2 x 10^6 = about 4.0 x 10^-4 m, i.e. about 0.4 mm.

questions.q: With the propagation of longitudinal waves through a medium, the quantity transmitted is: (a) matter, (b) energy, (c) energy and matter, (d) energy, matter and momentum.
questions.a: (b) Energy. The particles of the medium only oscillate about their mean positions; they are not carried along with the wave.

chapters.title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
points: Laws of chemical combination: law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier), law of definite proportions (Proust), law of multiple proportions (Dalton), Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes, Avogadro's law.
1 mole = 6.022 x 10^23 entities (Avogadro number) = molar mass in grams. Number of moles n = given mass / molar mass = given particles / N_A.
Empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio; molecular formula = n x empirical formula, where n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.
Percentage composition = (mass of element / molar mass) x 100. Limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first and decides the amount of product.
Concentration terms: molarity M = moles of solute / litres of solution; molality m = moles of solute / kg of solvent; mole fraction = moles of component / total moles.
Stoichiometry uses the balanced equation's mole ratio: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O means 2 mol H2 reacts with 1 mol O2.
Dalton's atomic theory: atoms are indestructible particles of an element; compounds form by combining atoms in simple whole-number ratios.

questions.q: Calculate the molar mass of the following: (i) H2O (ii) CO2 (iii) CH4.
questions.a: (i) 18.02 g/mol, (ii) 44.01 g/mol, (iii) 16.04 g/mol.

questions.q: Calculate the mass per cent of the different elements present in sodium sulphate (Na2SO4).
Calculate the atomic mass (average) of chlorine using: 35Cl (75.77%, 34.9689 amu), 37Cl (24.23%, 36.9659 amu).

Which of the following statements about a compound is INCORRECT: (i) A molecule of a compound has atoms of different elements. (ii) A compound retains the physical properties of its constituent elements. (iii) A compound cannot be separated into its constituent elements by physical methods. (iv) A compound is formed when atoms of different elements combine in a definite ratio.
questions.a: (ii) is incorrect - a compound's properties are entirely different from those of its constituent elements (e.g. NaCl vs Na and Cl).

chapters.title: Structure of Atom
points: Discovery: electron by Thomson (cathode rays, e/m measured), proton by Goldstein (anode rays), neutron by Chadwick (1932).

Rutherford's alpha-scattering: atom has a tiny dense positive nucleus; most mass is in the nucleus, most of the atom is empty space. Limitation: cannot explain stability (orbiting electrons should radiate and spiral in).
Bohr's model: electrons revolve in fixed orbits with angular momentum mvr = n h/(2pi). Energy of nth orbit for H: E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV. Radius r_n = 0.529 x n^2 Angstrom for H.
Bohr's model fails for multi-electron atoms and cannot explain spectral line splitting in magnetic fields (Zeeman effect).
de Broglie: every particle has wavelength lambda = h/(mv). Heisenberg uncertainty: delta x x delta p >= h/(4pi) - position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
Quantum numbers: n (principal: size/energy), l (azimuthal: shape of subshell, 0 to n-1), m (magnetic: orientation, -l to +l), s (spin: +1/2 or -1/2).

Aufbau principle (fill increasing n+l), Pauli exclusion (no two electrons share all 4 quantum numbers), Hund's rule (degenerate orbitals fill singly first). s, p, d, f subshells hold 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons.
Half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable: Cr is [Ar] 3d^5 4s^1 and Cu is [Ar] 3d^10 4s^1 instead of the expected configurations.

questions.q: Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the bromine isotope 80Br35.
questions.a: Protons = 35, electrons = 35 (neutral atom), neutrons = 80 - 35 = 45.

questions.q: The longest wavelength doublet absorption transition is observed at 589 and 589.6 nm. Calculate the frequency of each transition and the energy difference between the two excited states.
questions.a: nu1 = c/lambda1 = 5.093 x 10^14 s^-1; nu2 = 5.088 x 10^14 s^-1. Energy difference = h(nu1 - nu2) = about 3.3 x 10^-22 J.

questions.q: Electrons are emitted with zero velocity from a metal surface when it is exposed to radiation of wavelength 6800 Angstrom. Calculate the threshold frequency and the work function of the metal.
questions.a: Threshold frequency nu0 = c/lambda = 3 x 10^8/6800 x 10^-10 = 4.41 x 10^14 s^-1. Work function W0 = h nu0 = about 2.92 x 10^-19 J.

questions.q: Which of the following statements in relation to the hydrogen atom is correct: (i) 3s, 3p and 3d orbitals all have the same energy, (ii) 3s and 3p orbitals are of lower energy than 3d orbital, (iii) 3p orbital is lower in energy than 3d orbital, (iv) 3s orbital is lower in energy than 3p orbital.
questions.a: (i) In hydrogen, which has only one electron, the energy depends only on the principal quantum number n.

chapters.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
points: Modern periodic law: properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers (Moseley).
Long form of the periodic table: 7 periods (rows) and 18 groups (columns). Blocks: s (groups 1-2), p (13-18), d (transition metals), f (lanthanides/actinides).
Atomic radius decreases across a period (increasing effective nuclear charge pulls electrons in) and increases down a group (new shells are added).
Ionisation enthalpy: energy to remove an electron; increases across a period, decreases down a group. Be and N are higher than expected due to stable filled/half-filled subshells.

Electron gain enthalpy: energy released on adding an electron; generally increases across a period; chlorine has the highest (more than fluorine because F is very small and electron repulsion offsets attraction).
Electronegativity: tendency to attract shared electrons; increases across a period, decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
Diagonal relationship: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al (similar charge density) because trends oppose each other across and down.

questions.q: What is the basic theme of organisation in the periodic table?
questions.a: To simplify and systematise the study of elements and their compounds: elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals, so the properties are periodic functions of atomic number.

questions.q: Write the atomic number of the element present in the third period and seventeenth group of the periodic table.
questions.a: 17 - it is chlorine.

questions.q: Among the second period elements the actual ionisation enthalpies are in the order Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne. Explain why (i) Be has higher ionisation enthalpy than B, and (ii) O has lower ionisation enthalpy than N and F.
questions.a: (i) Be loses its 2s electron, which penetrates closer to the nucleus; B loses a 2p electron, which is higher in energy. (ii) N has a stable half-filled 2p^3 configuration, so removing an electron costs more; O loses one electron to reach that stable half-filled arrangement. F has the highest effective nuclear charge of the three.

questions.q: Consider the isoelectronic species Na+, Mg2+, F- and O2-. The correct order of increasing radii is: (i) F- < O2- < Mg2+ < Na+ (ii) Mg2+ < Na+ < F- < O2- (iii) O2- < F- < Na+ < Mg2+ (iv) O2- < F- < Mg2+ < Na+
questions.a: (ii) Mg2+ < Na+ < F- < O2-. All have 10 electrons; higher nuclear charge pulls the same electron cloud in more strongly.

chapters.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
points: Ionic bond: complete electron transfer from metal to non-metal; lattice energy holds the crystal (e.g. NaCl). Conducts electricity only in molten/aqueous state.
Covalent bond: electron sharing; formed by orbital overlap - sigma bonds (axial overlap, stronger) and pi bonds (sideways overlap).

VSEPR theory: electron pairs arrange to minimise repulsion; lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair repulsion. Shapes: linear (2 bp), trigonal planar (3), tetrahedral (4), e. NH3 is pyramidal and H2O is bent due to lone pairs.
Hybridisation: sp (linear, 180 deg, e. CO2), sp2 (trigonal planar, 120 deg, e. BF3), sp3 (tetrahedral, 109.5 deg, e. CH4).
Molecular orbital theory: bonding MOs lower energy, antibonding MOs raise it; bond order = (N_b - N_a)/2. Bond order zero means no stable molecule.
Dipole moment measures bond polarity; molecules with symmetric shapes (CO2, CCl4) have zero net dipole. Hydrogen bonding (H bonded to F, O, N) gives water and ice their special properties.
Resonance: delocalised electrons shown by multiple Lewis structures (e. benzene, O3); the true structure is a hybrid with bond lengths between single and double.

questions.q: Explain the formation of a chemical bond.
questions.a: A chemical bond is the attractive force that holds atoms together in a molecule. Atoms combine to form molecules because the energy of the system is lower (more stable) when they are bonded than when the atoms are far apart.

questions.q: Explain why the BeH2 molecule has a zero dipole moment although the Be-H bonds are polar.
questions.a: BeH2 is linear: the two equal and opposite Be-H bond dipoles cancel each other exactly, giving zero net dipole moment.

questions.q: Although both CO2 and H2O are triatomic molecules, the shape of H2O is bent while that of CO2 is linear. Explain this on the basis of dipole moment.
questions.a: CO2 has zero dipole moment, so its two bond moments cancel - the molecule must be linear. H2O has a net dipole moment of 1.85 D, so its bond moments do not cancel - the molecule is bent.

questions.q: Isostructural species are those which have the same shape and hybridisation. Among the given species, identify the isostructural pair: (a) NF3 and BF3 (b) BF4- and NH4+ (c) BCl3 and BrCl3 (d) NH3 and NO3-
questions.a: (b) BF4- and NH4+: both are tetrahedral.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
points: System types: open (exchanges matter and energy), closed (energy only), isolated (neither). State functions (U, H, S, G) depend only on the state, not the path; heat and work are path functions.
First law: delta U = q + w (chemistry sign convention: work done ON the system is positive). Enthalpy H = U + PV; at constant pressure delta H = q_p.
Enthalpy changes: delta_f H (formation), delta_c H (combustion), Hess's law (delta H of a reaction is the sum of delta H of its steps, independent of path).
Bond enthalpies estimate delta H: sum of (bonds broken) minus sum of (bonds formed).
Entropy S measures disorder; delta S = q_rev / T. Spontaneous processes increase total entropy of the universe.
Gibbs free energy: delta G = delta H - T delta S. Reaction is spontaneous when delta G < 0; at equilibrium delta G = 0 and delta G = -RT ln K.
A reaction is always spontaneous when delta H < 0 and delta S > 0; it becomes spontaneous at high temperature when delta H > 0 and delta S > 0 (T > delta H / delta S).

questions.q: Choose the correct answer. A thermodynamic state function is a quantity: (i) used to determine heat changes (ii) whose value is independent of path (iii) used to determine pressure-volume work (iv) whose value depends on temperature only.
questions.a: (ii) A state function depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken.

questions.q: For a process to occur under adiabatic conditions, the correct condition is: (i) delta T = 0 (ii) delta p = 0 (iii) q = 0 (iv) w = 0
questions.a: (iii) q = 0 - no heat enters or leaves the system.

questions.q: Enthalpies of formation of CO(g), CO2(g), N2O(g) and N2O4(g) are -110, -393, 81 and 9.7 kJ/mol respectively. Find the value of delta_rH for: N2O4(g) + 3CO(g) -> N2O(g) + 3CO2(g).

Thermodynamics is not concerned about: (i) energy changes involved in a chemical reaction, (ii) the extent to which a chemical reaction proceeds, (iii) the rate at which a reaction proceeds, (iv) the feasibility of a chemical reaction.
questions.a: (iii) Thermodynamics says nothing about how fast a reaction happens - that is the domain of chemical kinetics.

chapters.title: Equilibrium
points: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations stay constant though reactions continue (e., in a closed vessel H2 + I2 <=> 2HI).
Law of mass action: for aA + bB <=> cC + dD, K_c = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). K_p uses partial pressures; K_p = K_c (RT)^(delta n).
Reaction quotient Q compares with K: if Q < K the reaction moves forward; if Q > K it moves backward; Q = K at equilibrium.

Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change - increasing reactant concentration, pressure (towards fewer gas moles), or lowering temperature for exothermic reactions favours products.
Acids donate H+ (Bronsted-Lowry) or accept electron pairs (Lewis); conjugate acid-base pairs differ by one H+. Water is amphiprotic.
pH = -log [H+]; pOH = -log [OH-]; at 25 deg C pH + pOH = 14 and K_w = 10^-14. Buffer solutions resist pH change (weak acid + its salt, or weak base + its salt).
Solubility product K_sp: for a sparingly soluble salt, precipitation occurs when the ionic product exceeds K_sp (common ion effect lowers solubility).

questions.q: A liquid is in equilibrium with its vapour in a sealed container at a fixed temperature. The volume of the container is suddenly increased. (a) What is the initial effect on vapour pressure? (b) How do the rates of evaporation and condensation change initially? (c) What happens when equilibrium is restored finally, and what will be the final vapour pressure?
questions.a: (a) Vapour pressure falls initially as the same vapour spreads over a larger volume. (b) Evaporation increases and condensation decreases. (c) More liquid evaporates until equilibrium is restored; the final vapour pressure equals the original value, since it depends only on temperature.

questions.q: The pH of a sample of vinegar is 3.76. Calculate the concentration of hydrogen ions in it.
The ionisation constants of HF, HCOOH and HCN at 298 K are 6.8 x 10^-4, 1.8 x 10^-4 and 4.8 x 10^-9 respectively. Calculate the ionisation constants of their conjugate bases.
For the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g), the standard free energy change delta G0 is greater than zero. The equilibrium constant K would be: (i) K = 0 (ii) K > 1 (iii) K = 1 (iv) K < 1
questions.a: (iv) K < 1, since delta G0 = -RT ln K; a positive delta G0 means ln K is negative.

chapters.title: Redox Reactions
points: Oxidation = loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number); reduction = gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). They always occur together.

Oxidation number rules: free elements 0; Group 1 metals +1; Group 2 +2; F -1; O usually -2 (except -1 in peroxides, +2 in OF2); H usually +1 (except -1 in metal hydrides). Sum of oxidation numbers equals the charge of the species.
Oxidising agents accept electrons (get reduced): e. KMnO4, K2Cr2O7. Reducing agents donate electrons (get oxidised): e. metals, H2, C.

Balancing redox reactions: ion-electron (half-reaction) method - split into oxidation and reduction halves, balance atoms (O with H2O, H with H+ in acidic medium), balance charge with electrons, then combine.
Disproportionation: the same element is both oxidised and reduced (e. Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O; here Cl goes from 0 to -1 and +1).
Electrochemical series: metals above hydrogen displace H2 from acids; a metal higher in the series displaces one below it from its salt solution.

questions.q: Assign the oxidation number to Mn in K2MnO4.
questions.a: Let it be x: 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 gives x = +6.

questions.q: Consider the elements Cs, Ne, I and F. (a) Identify the element that exhibits only negative oxidation state. (b) The element that exhibits only positive oxidation state. (c) The element that exhibits both positive and negative oxidation states. (d) The element which exhibits neither negative nor positive oxidation state.
questions.a: (a) F (b) Cs (c) I (d) Ne.

questions.q: The compound AgF2 is unstable. However, if formed, it acts as a very strong oxidising agent. Why?
questions.a: Ag(II) is unstable and readily gains one electron to become the stable Ag(I); the strong tendency to be reduced makes AgF2 a powerful oxidising agent.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a redox reaction: (i) CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O (ii) Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 (iii) 2K + F2 -> 2KF (iv) BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl
questions.a: (iv) - it is a double displacement (precipitation) reaction with no change in oxidation numbers.

chapters.title: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
points: Tetravalency of carbon (Kekule) and catenation: carbon forms 4 covalent bonds and long chains, giving millions of organic compounds.
Functional groups decide a compound's chemistry: -OH (alcohol), -CHO (aldehyde), -CO- (ketone), -COOH (carboxylic acid), -NH2 (amine), -X (halide).
IUPAC naming: choose the longest chain containing the principal functional group, number to give it the lowest locant; prefixes for substituents in alphabetical order (e., 2-methylbutane).
Structural isomerism: chain (butane vs 2-methylpropane), position (1-propanol vs 2-propanol), functional (ethanol vs dimethyl ether), metamerism, tautomerism (keto-enol).
Electronic effects: inductive effect (electronegativity-based, permanent), electromeric effect (temporary, on attack), resonance/mesomeric effect (delocalisation), hyperconjugation.
Carbocation stability: 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg (hyperconjugation + inductive); carbanion stability is the reverse. Free radicals follow carbocation order.
Purification: distillation (liquids), fractional distillation, crystallisation (solids), chromatography, sublimation (e. camphor), steam distillation for steam-volatile compounds.
Qualitative analysis: Lassaigne's test - N gives Prussian blue, S gives violet with nitroprusside, halogens give AgX precipitate. Quantitative: Kjeldahl (N), Carius (halogen/S).

questions.q: What are the hybridisation states of each carbon atom in CH2=C=O?
questions.a: The CH2 carbon is sp2 hybridised (two sigma bonds + one pi); the central carbon joined to C and O is sp hybridised.

questions.q: Indicate the sigma and pi bonds in CH2=C=CH2 (allene).
questions.a: 4 C-H sigma + 2 C-C sigma = 6 sigma bonds; 2 pi bonds (one on each C=C).

questions.q: Explain the terms inductive and electromeric effects. Which electron displacement effect explains the correct acidity order: Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH?
questions.a: The inductive effect is the permanent polarisation of sigma bonds by electronegative atoms; the electromeric effect is a temporary shift of pi electrons under attack by a reagent. The -I effect of the Cl atoms explains the acidity order - more Cl atoms pull electron density away and stabilise the carboxylate ion.

questions.q: The principle involved in paper chromatography is: (i) adsorption (ii) partition (iii) solubility (iv) volatility
questions.a: (ii) Partition - the components distribute between the stationary (water held on paper) and mobile phases.

chapters.title: Hydrocarbons
points: Alkanes (CnH2n+2): saturated, sp3. Preparation: hydrogenation of alkenes/alkynes, Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na -> R-R), decarboxylation of sodium salts (soda lime: RCOONa + NaOH -> RH). Reactions: free-radical halogenation (reactivity 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg H), combustion, pyrolysis/cracking.

Alkenes (CnH2n): contain C=C, sp2. Preparation: dehydration of alcohols (conc. H2SO4, Saytzeff product major), dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides. Reactions: electrophilic addition - H2, X2, HX (Markovnikov: H adds to the carbon with more H already), hydration, ozonolysis (cleaves double bond).

Alkynes (CnH2n-2): C triple C, sp. Acetylene from CaC2 + H2O. Terminal alkynes are acidic (pKa about 25): RC triple CH + NaNH2 -> salt; gives red precipitate with ammoniacal Cu2Cl2 and white with AgNO3. Addition of HX twice (Markovnikov), hydration gives methyl ketones (Hg2+/H2SO4).

Benzene: aromatic, planar hexagon with delocalised pi electrons; Huckel rule (4n+2 pi electrons) explains stability. Electrophilic substitution: nitration (conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 -> nitrobenzene), halogenation (FeX3), sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation (AlCl3).
Directing effects: -OH, -NH2, -CH3 are ortho/para directors and activators; -NO2, -CHO, -COOH are meta directors and deactivators (halogens are ortho/para but deactivating).
Conformations of ethane: staggered is more stable than eclipsed (torsional strain); energy difference about 12.5 kJ/mol. Sawhorse and Newman projections show them.
Markovnikov's rule explained by the most stable carbocation intermediate; peroxide effect (Kharasch) reverses it only for HBr addition.

questions.q: How will you convert ethyne into benzene?
questions.a: Pass ethyne (acetylene) through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K: 3 HC triple-bond CH -> C6H6 (cyclic polymerisation).

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names of the products obtained by the ozonolysis of pent-2-ene.
questions.a: Ethanal (CH3CHO) and propanal (CH3CH2CHO) - the double bond breaks to give one aldehyde from each side.

questions.q: Draw the cis and trans structures of hex-2-ene. Which isomer has the higher boiling point, and why?
questions.a: The cis isomer has the higher boiling point: its dipole moment is larger, giving stronger dipole-dipole attraction than in the nearly non-polar trans form.

questions.q: Arrange the following hydrogen halides in order of their decreasing reactivity with propene: (i) HCl > HBr > HI (ii) HBr > HI > HCl (iii) HI > HBr > HCl (iv) HCl > HI > HBr
questions.a: (iii) HI > HBr > HCl - as the halogen size increases, the H-X bond weakens, so the proton is donated more easily in electrophilic addition.

chapters.title: Sets
points: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. Roster form lists elements: A = {1, 2, 3}; set-builder form: A = {x : x is a natural number less than 4}.
Subsets: A is a subset of B if every element of A is in B. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets and 2^n - 1 proper subsets. Power set P(A) is the set of all subsets.
Operations: union A u B, intersection A n B, difference A - B, complement A' (elements of universal set not in A).
De Morgan's laws: (A u B)' = A' n B'; (A n B)' = A' u B'.
For finite sets: n(A u B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B); n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(B n C) - n(C n A) + n(A n B n C).
Intervals: open (a, b), closed [a, b], half-open [a, b). Empty set phi has zero elements and is a subset of every set.

questions.q: Whether the following is a set or not: (i) The collection of all months of a year beginning with the letter J. (ii) The collection of the ten most talented writers of India.
questions.a: (i) It is a set: January, June, July are well defined. (ii) It is not a set: 'most talented' is not well defined.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}. Find A union B.
Let X and Y be sets such that n(X) = 17, n(Y) = 23 and n(X union Y) = 38. Find n(X intersection Y).
questions.a: n(X intersection Y) = 17 + 23 - 38 = 2.

questions.q: Let A and B be two sets. Then A intersection (A union B) is equal to: (A) A (B) B (C) null set (D) A intersection B
questions.a: (A) A. Absorption law: A is a subset of A union B, so the intersection with A is A itself.

chapters.title: Relations and Functions
points: Ordered pair (a, b): order matters. Cartesian product A x B = {(a, b) : a in A, b in B}; if n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A x B) = pq.
Relation R from A to B is a subset of A x B. Domain = set of first elements; range = set of second elements.
Function f: A -> B assigns each element of A exactly one element of B. Domain, co-domain, range: range is a subset of the co-domain.
Types: one-one (injective: distinct inputs give distinct outputs), onto (surjective: range = co-domain), one-one onto (bijective).
Standard functions: identity f(x) = x; constant f(x) = c; polynomial; rational; modulus f(x) = |x|; signum; greatest integer f(x) = [x].
Algebra of functions: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x), (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x), (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) where g(x) is not zero.

questions.q: If (x + 1, y - 2) = (3, 1), find the values of x and y.
questions.a: x + 1 = 3 gives x = 2; y - 2 = 1 gives y = 3.

questions.q: Let P = {a, b, c} and Q = {r}. Are P x Q and Q x P equal?
questions.a: No. P x Q = {(a,r), (b,r), (c,r)} while Q x P = {(r,a), (r,b), (r,c)}; the ordered pairs differ.

questions.q: Find the domain and range of the real function f(x) = sqrt(9 - x^2).
questions.a: Domain: -3 <= x <= 3, i.e. [-3, 3]. Range: [0, 3], since sqrt preserves non-negative values and 9 - x^2 is at most 9.
(D) x can take -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (x^2 must be at most 8); e.g. x = 2 works with y = +/-1.

chapters.title: Trigonometric Functions
points: Angle in radians = arc length / radius; 1 radian = 57.3 degrees (approx). 360 deg = 2pi radians; to convert: radians = degrees x pi/180.
ASTC rule by quadrant: I (all positive), II (sin positive), III (tan positive), IV (cos positive). sin(-x) = -sin x; cos(-x) = cos x; tan(-x) = -tan x.
Key identities: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1; 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x; 1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x.
Compound angles: sin(A+B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B; cos(A+B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B; tan(A+B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B).
Double angles: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2sin^2 A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A).
Product to sum: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B); 2 cos A sin B = sin(A+B) - sin(A-B); cos^2 A = (1 + cos 2A)/2.
Sum to product: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2); cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2).

questions.q: Find the exact value of sin 75 degrees.
questions.a: sin 75 = sin(45 + 30) = sin45 cos30 + cos45 sin30 = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4.

questions.q: Convert 240 degrees into radian measure.
questions.a: 240 x pi/180 = 4pi/3 radians.

questions.q: Convert 7pi/6 into degree measure.
questions.a: 7pi/6 x 180/pi = 210 degrees.

questions.q: A wheel makes 360 revolutions in one minute. Through how many radians does it turn in one second?
questions.a: 360 revolutions/min = 6 revolutions/s, so it turns 6 x 2pi = 12pi radians per second.

chapters.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
points: i = sqrt(-1), with i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1. A complex number z = a + ib has real part a and imaginary part b; modulus |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Conjugate of a + ib is a - ib; z x conjugate(z) = |z|^2. To divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
Argand plane: real axis (x) and imaginary axis (y); z = a + ib is the point (a, b); |z| is its distance from origin.
Argument theta = tan^-1(b/a) (adjusted by quadrant). Polar form: z = r(cos theta + i sin theta), where r = |z|.
Algebra: (a+ib) + (c+id) = (a+c) + i(b+d); (a+ib)(c+id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc).
Quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = 0 has roots x = (-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a). Discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac: D > 0 two real roots; D = 0 equal roots; D < 0 complex conjugate roots.
Sum of roots = -b/a, product of roots = c/a. A quadratic with roots alpha, beta is x^2 - (sum)x + (product) = 0.

questions.q: Express (5i)(-3i/5) in the form a + ib.
Find the multiplicative inverse of 4 - 3i.
Find the modulus and argument of -1 - i sqrt(3).
questions.a: Modulus = 2. Argument = -2pi/3 (the point lies in the third quadrant, and the principal argument is taken between -pi and pi).

questions.q: The value of i^-39 is: (A) 1 (B) -1 (C) i (D) -i

chapters.title: Linear Inequalities
points: Inequality rules: adding/subtracting the same number keeps the sense; multiplying/dividing by a positive number keeps it, by a negative number reverses it.
Solving ax + b > 0: e. 2x - 6 > 0 gives x > 3. Solution sets are intervals on the number line.
Quadratic inequalities: factor and use a sign chart. x^2 - 4 > 0 gives x < -2 or x > 2.
Absolute value: |x| < a means -a < x < a; |x| > a means x < -a or x > a.
Two-variable inequalities ax + by > c: the boundary line ax + by = c divides the plane; test the origin to find the solution half-plane.
System of inequalities: solution is the intersection (common region) of all individual solution sets, found graphically.

questions.q: Solve 24x < 100, when (i) x is a natural number, (ii) x is an integer.
Solve -12x > 30, when (i) x is a natural number, (ii) x is an integer.
questions.a: Dividing by -12 reverses the inequality: x < -30/12 = -2.5. (i) No natural number solution. (ii) Integers ..., -5, -4, -3, i.e. x <= -3.

questions.q: |x| < 3 is equivalent to: (A) x >= 3 (B) -3 < x < 3 (C) x <= -3 (D) -3 <= x <= 3

chapters.title: Permutations and Combinations
points: Fundamental principle of counting: if one task has m ways and another has n ways, both together have m x n ways.
Factorial: n! = n(n-1)...2x1; 0! = 1. Permutations (order matters): nPr = n! / (n-r)!; combinations (order irrelevant): nCr = n! / (r!(n-r)!).
nPr counts arrangements (seating, passwords); nCr counts selections (committees, teams).
Key results: nCr = nC(n-r); nC0 = nCn = 1; nC1 = n; nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr (Pascal's rule).
Permutations of n objects with p, q identical among them: n! / (p! q!).
Circular arrangements: (n-1)! for n distinct objects around a circle.

questions.q: Given 5 flags of different colours, how many different signals can be generated if each signal requires the use of 2 flags, one below the other?
questions.a: 5 x 4 = 20 signals.

questions.q: From a committee of 8 persons, how many ways can a chairman and a vice-chairman be chosen, one person not holding more than one position?
questions.a: 8 choices for chairman, then 7 for vice-chairman: 8 x 7 = 56 ways.

questions.q: If (n-1)P3 : nP4 = 1 : 9, find n.
questions.a: Solving (n-1)!/(n-4)! divided by n!/(n-4)! = 1/9 gives (n-1)/n(n-1)... leads to n = 9.

questions.q: If nC12 = nC8, then n is equal to: (A) 20 (B) 12 (C) 6 (D) 30
questions.a: (A) 20, since nCr = nCs implies r = s or r + s = n; here 12 + 8 = 20.

chapters.title: Binomial Theorem
points: Binomial theorem: (a + b)^n = sum over r of nCr a^(n-r) b^r, for r = 0 to n. There are n+1 terms.
General term: T_(r+1) = nCr a^(n-r) b^r. Middle term(s): if n is even, the ((n/2)+1)th term; if n is odd, two middle terms.
Coefficients are symmetric: nCr = nC(n-r). Sum of all binomial coefficients = 2^n.
(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + nC2 x^2 + ...; putting x = 1 and x = -1 gives useful coefficient sums.
Greatest binomial coefficient: for even n it is nC(n/2); for odd n both nC((n-1)/2) and nC((n+1)/2).

questions.q: Expand (1 - 2x)^5 using the binomial theorem.
Expand (2/x - x/2)^5.
Find the middle terms in the expansion of (3 - x^3/6)^7.
questions.a: There are 8 terms, so the middle terms are the 4th and 5th: -105x^9/8 and 35x^12/48.

questions.q: The largest coefficient in the expansion of (1 + x)^30 is: (A) 30C15 (B) 30C10 (C) 30C20 (D) 30C30
questions.a: (A) 30C15 - the middle coefficient of a binomial row is the largest.

chapters.title: Sequences and Series
points: Arithmetic progression: a, a+d, a+2d...; nth term a_n = a + (n-1)d; sum S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n-1)d) = (n/2)(first + last).
Geometric progression: a, ar, ar^2...; nth term a_n = a r^(n-1); sum S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1). For |r| < 1, infinite sum S_inf = a/(1 - r).
Arithmetic mean of a and b: (a+b)/2. Geometric mean: sqrt(ab). AM >= GM for positive numbers.
Relation between AM, GM, HM: AM >= GM >= HM; GM^2 = AM x HM.
Special sums: sum k = n(n+1)/2; sum k^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6; sum k^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2.
A series converges to a finite sum only if its terms tend to zero (necessary but not sufficient); the infinite GP sum formula needs |r| < 1.

questions.q: Find the first five terms of the sequence a_n = 3n + 2.
Find the 20th term and the nth term of the GP 5/2, 5/4, 5/8, ...
Which term of the sequence 2, 2sqrt2, 4, ... is 128?
questions.a: Common ratio sqrt2, and 128 = 2^7 = 2 x (sqrt2)^12: so 128 is the 13th term.

questions.q: Find the sum to n terms of the series: 1 x 2 + 2 x 3 + 3 x 4 + ...

chapters.title: Straight Lines
points: Slope m = tan theta = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), where theta is the angle with the positive x-axis. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m1 x m2 = -1.
Forms: point-slope y - y1 = m(x - x1); slope-intercept y = mx + c; two-point form; intercept form x/a + y/b = 1; normal form x cos alpha + y sin alpha = p.
General equation: Ax + By + C = 0 has slope -A/B and intercepts (-C/A, -C/B).
Angle between lines with slopes m1, m2: tan theta = |(m1 - m2)/(1 + m1 m2)|.
Distance of point (x1, y1) from line Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax1 + By1 + C| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2). Distance between parallel lines differs only in C.
Concurrency: three lines are concurrent if they pass through one point; check using determinants or by solving two and substituting in the third.

questions.q: Find the area of the quadrilateral whose vertices are (-4, 5), (0, 7), (5, -5) and (-4, -2), taken in order.
questions.a: Using the shoelace formula: (1/2)|-58 - 63| = 60.5 square units.

questions.q: An equilateral triangle has side length 2a. Its base lies on the y-axis with the midpoint at the origin. Find the vertices of the triangle.
questions.a: (0, a), (0, -a) and (sqrt3 a, 0); equivalently the third vertex may be (-sqrt3 a, 0).

questions.q: Find the distance between P(x1, y1) and Q(x2, y2) when (i) PQ is parallel to the y-axis, (ii) PQ is parallel to the x-axis.
The equation of the line through the point (1, 2) and perpendicular to the line x + y + 1 = 0 is: (A) y - x + 1 = 0 (B) y - x - 1 = 0 (C) y - x + 2 = 0 (D) y - x - 2 = 0
questions.a: (B) y - x - 1 = 0. Slope of the given line is -1, so the perpendicular has slope 1: y - 2 = 1(x - 1).

chapters.title: Conic Sections
points: Circle: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. General form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
Parabola: set of points equidistant from focus and directrix; standard form y^2 = 4ax (focus (a, 0), directrix x = -a).
Ellipse: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (a > b); foci at (+-c, 0) with c^2 = a^2 - b^2; eccentricity e = c/a < 1; latus rectum = 2b^2/a.
Hyperbola: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1; foci at (+-c, 0) with c^2 = a^2 + b^2; e > 1; asymptotes y = +- (b/a)x.
Eccentricity identifies the conic: e = 0 circle, e = 1 parabola, 0 < e < 1 ellipse, e > 1 hyperbola.
Parametric points: circle (r cos theta, r sin theta); ellipse (a cos theta, b sin theta).

questions.q: Find the equation of the circle with centre (0, 2) and radius 2.
Find the coordinates of the focus, the axis, the equation of the directrix and the length of the latus rectum of the parabola y^2 = 12x.
questions.a: 4a = 12, so a = 3. Focus = (3, 0); axis is the x-axis; directrix x = -3; length of latus rectum = 12.

questions.q: Find the coordinates of the foci, the vertices, the lengths of the major and minor axes, the eccentricity and the length of the latus rectum of the ellipse x^2/36 + y^2/16 = 1.
questions.a: a = 6, b = 4, c = 2 sqrt5. Foci (±2 sqrt5, 0); vertices (±6, 0); major axis 12; minor axis 8; e = sqrt5/3; latus rectum = 16/3.

questions.q: The area of the triangle formed by the vertex and the ends of the latus rectum of the parabola x^2 = 12y is: (A) 16 (B) 18 (C) 24 (D) 36 square units
questions.a: (B) 18. a = 3; latus rectum = 12, focal distance = 3, so area = (1/2)(12)(3) = 18.

chapters.title: Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry
points: A point in 3D is (x, y, z): x, y, z are distances from the YZ, XZ, XY planes respectively. The eight octants are the 3D analogue of quadrants.
Distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2): sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2 + (z2-z1)^2).
Distance of (x, y, z) from the origin: sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). Distance from coordinate planes: |x| from YZ, |y| from XZ, |z| from XY.
Section formula: point dividing the join of (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2) in ratio m:n is ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n), (mz2+nz1)/(m+n)); midpoint uses m = n = 1.
Centroid of triangle with vertices (x1,y1,z1), (x2,y2,z2), (x3,y3,z3): the average of the coordinates.

questions.q: A point is on the x-axis. What are its y-coordinate and z-coordinate?
questions.a: Both are 0: a point on the x-axis has the form (x, 0, 0).

questions.q: Find the distance between the points (2, 3, 5) and (4, 3, 1).
Find the distance between the points (-1, 3, -4) and (1, -3, 4).
The distance of the point P(3, 4, 5) from the y-axis is: (A) sqrt34 (B) sqrt41 (C) 4 (D) 5
questions.a: (A) sqrt34: drop the perpendicular to the y-axis; the distance is sqrt(3^2 + 5^2) = sqrt34.

chapters.title: Limits and Derivatives
points: Limit: lim x->a f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a. Direct substitution works when the function is continuous there.
Standard limits: lim x->0 sin x / x = 1; lim x->0 (e^x - 1)/x = 1; lim x->0 (a^x - 1)/x = ln a; lim x->0 (1+x)^(1/x) = e; lim x->a (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n-1).
Algebra of limits: limit of sum/product/quotient = sum/product/quotient of limits (denominator not zero). Factorise or rationalise to remove 0/0 forms.
Derivative: f'(x) = lim h->0 [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h (first principle). Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent at that point.
Rules: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1); (u+v)' = u' + v'; (uv)' = u'v + uv'; (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2; chain rule dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx.
Derivatives of trig functions: (sin x)' = cos x; (cos x)' = -sin x; (tan x)' = sec^2 x.

questions.q: Evaluate lim as x -> 3 of (x + 3).
questions.a: Substituting x = 3 gives 6.

questions.q: Evaluate lim as x -> 0 of (cos 2x - 1)/(cos x - 1).
questions.a: Use cos 2x - 1 = -2 sin^2 x and cos x - 1 = -2 sin^2(x/2): the limit is 4.

questions.q: Find the derivative of x^2 - 2 at x = 10 from first principles (or directly).
questions.a: d/dx(x^2 - 2) = 2x, so at x = 10 the derivative is 20.

questions.q: lim as x -> pi of sin x/(x - pi) is equal to: (A) 1 (B) 2 (C) -1 (D) -2
questions.a: (C) -1. Put t = x - pi: sin x = -sin t, and sin t/t -> 1.

chapters.title: Statistics
points: Measures of central tendency: mean, median, mode. Measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation, variance, standard deviation.
Mean deviation about mean = (sum |x_i - xbar|) / n; about median uses median in place of mean.
Variance sigma^2 = (sum (x_i - xbar)^2) / n = (sum x_i^2)/n - (xbar)^2. Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance).
For grouped data: mean = sum f_i x_i / sum f_i; variance = (sum f_i x_i^2 / N) - (mean)^2.
Coefficient of variation CV = (sigma / xbar) x 100: smaller CV means more consistent data - used to compare two series.
Standard deviation is independent of origin (shifting data doesn't change it) but scales with change of scale: if y = ax + b, sigma_y = |a| sigma_x.

questions.q: Find the mean deviation about the mean for the numbers 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 17.
questions.a: Mean = 10. Sum of absolute deviations = 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 3 + 7 = 24; mean deviation = 24/8 = 3.

questions.q: Find the mean and the variance of the numbers 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 4, 8, 12.
questions.a: Mean = 9. Sum of squared deviations = 74, so variance = 74/8 = 9.25.

questions.q: Calculate the mean and the variance for the frequency distribution: x: 6, 10, 14, 18, 24, 28, 30 and f: 2, 4, 7, 12, 8, 4, 3.
questions.a: Sum fx = 760 over N = 40, so mean = 19. Sum fx^2 = 16176, variance = 16176/40 - 19^2 = 43.4.

questions.q: Mean deviation from the mean for the values 3, 10, 10, 4, 7, 10, 5 is: (A) 2 (B) 2.57 (C) 3 (D) 3.75
questions.a: (B) 2.57. Mean = 7; absolute deviations 4, 3, 3, 3, 0, 3, 2 sum to 18, and 18/7 = 2.57.

chapters.title: Probability
points: Random experiment: outcome not predictable in advance. Sample space S = set of all possible outcomes; an event is a subset of S.
Probability of event E: P(E) = n(E) / n(S) for equally likely outcomes; 0 <= P(E) <= 1; P(impossible) = 0, P(sure) = 1.
Complement: P(not E) = 1 - P(E). Addition rule: P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B); for mutually exclusive events P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B).
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together (A n B = phi); exhaustive events cover the whole sample space.
For two dice: sample space has 36 outcomes; P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6; P(doublet) = 6/36 = 1/6.
P(at least one) = 1 - P(none) is often the fastest route in 'at least' problems.

questions.q: A coin is tossed twice. What is the probability that at least one tail occurs?
questions.a: Sample space {HH, HT, TH, TT}; favourable outcomes = 3, so P = 3/4.

questions.q: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting (i) a prime number, (ii) a number greater than 6.
questions.a: (i) Primes are 2, 3, 5, so P = 3/6 = 1/2. (ii) 0 - no face exceeds 6.

questions.q: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Calculate the probability that the card will (i) be an ace of spades, (ii) be an ace, (iii) be a black card.
If P(A union B) = P(A intersection B) then: (A) P(A) = P(B) (B) P(A) > P(B) (C) P(A) < P(B) (D) none of these
questions.a: (A) P(A) = P(B). Since P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A intersection B), equality forces P(A) + P(B) = 2P(A intersection B), which (with P(A intersect B) <= each) gives P(A) = P(B).

chapters.title: The Living World
points: Defining properties of living beings: growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and consciousness (ability to sense the environment).
Biodiversity: about 1.7-1.8 million species have been identified and described so far; many more await discovery.
Taxonomy is the classification, identification and nomenclature of organisms. Systematics also includes evolutionary relationships (Linnaeus is called the father of taxonomy).

Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each name has two parts - genus (capital first letter) and specific epithet (lowercase). Names are in Latin, written in italics (or underlined when handwritten).
Taxonomic hierarchy (broad to narrow): Kingdom > Phylum/Division > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species. Species is the basic unit; taxa with fewer ranks share more common features.
Example: mango - Kingdom Plantae, Division Angiospermae, Class Dicotyledonae, Order Sapindales, Family Anacardiaceae, Genus Mangifera, Species indica.

questions.q: Why are living organisms classified?
questions.a: Classification makes it convenient to study the enormous diversity of living beings: it groups organisms with common characteristics so their study becomes systematic.

questions.q: Why do classification systems continue to change over time?
questions.a: Because new organisms are discovered and new techniques (cytotaxonomy, chemotaxonomy, DNA studies) keep revealing new relationships, so the criteria and systems keep being refined.

questions.q: If you were to identify and classify the people you meet often, what criteria would you use (say, at least ten)?
questions.a: Age, sex, height, weight, skin colour, education, profession, income and marital status - any set of useful, observable characters serves for a workable classification.

questions.q: As we go from species to kingdom in a taxonomic hierarchy, the number of common characteristics: (a) will decrease (b) will increase (c) remain the same (d) may increase or decrease, depending on the number of taxa used.
questions.a: (a) Will decrease. Lower categories share more characters; higher taxa are united on fewer, broader characteristics.

chapters.title: Biological Classification
points: R. Whittaker (1969) proposed the five-kingdom system: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia - based on cell structure, body organisation, nutrition and phylogeny.

Monera: prokaryotic bacteria; cell wall has peptidoglycan. Includes archaebacteria (extreme habitats), eubacteria (true bacteria), cyanobacteria (photosynthetic, e. Nostoc, Anabaena - nitrogen fixers).

Protista: single-celled eukaryotes - Chrysophytes (diatoms, golden algae; chief ocean producers), Dinoflagellates (e. Gonyaulax causes red tides), Euglenoids (Euglena - mixotroph), Slime moulds, Protozoans (Amoeba, Paramoecium, Plasmodium - malarial parasite).
Fungi: eukaryotic, heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin. Classes: Phycomycetes (Mucor), Ascomycetes (yeast, Penicillium), Basidiomycetes (Agaricus mushroom), Deuteromycetes (Alternaria).

Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites with protein coat (capsid); they are inert outside a host - not placed in the five-kingdom system. Viroids (Diener) are naked RNA; prions are infectious proteins; lichens are symbiosis of alga + fungus.

questions.q: How have classification systems of organisms changed over time?
questions.a: They expanded from two kingdoms (Linnaeus) to three, four and finally Whittaker's five kingdoms, as study criteria broadened from morphology to cell structure, mode of nutrition and evolutionary relationships.

questions.q: Give two economically important uses of (i) heterotrophic bacteria and (ii) archaebacteria.
questions.a: (i) Heterotrophic bacteria: making curd and antibiotics, and Rhizobium fixing nitrogen in legume fields. (ii) Archaebacteria: methanogens in gobar gas (biogas) plants and in the rumen of ruminants, helping cellulose digestion.

questions.q: State the structure and genetic material present in viruses. Name four viruses and the diseases they cause.
questions.a: A virus has a protein capsid surrounding nucleic acid (DNA or RNA), sometimes with a lipid envelope. Examples: TMV (tobacco mosaic), HIV (AIDS), Variola virus (smallpox), Influenza virus (flu).

questions.q: All eukaryotic unicellular organisms belong to: (a) Monera (b) Protista (c) Fungi (d) Bacteria
questions.a: (b) Protista.

chapters.title: Plant Kingdom
points: Algae: chlorophyllous simple plants, mostly aquatic. Green algae (Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra), brown algae (Laminaria, Fucus - contain fucoxanthin), red algae (Polysiphonia, Gelidium - source of agar).
Algae provide at least half of the Earth's total CO2 fixation through photosynthesis.

Bryophytes: amphibians of the plant kingdom (need water for fertilisation); no true vascular tissue; main plant body is haploid gametophyte. Examples: Funaria (moss), Marchantia (liverwort), Sphagnum (peat moss).
Pteridophytes: first terrestrial plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem); main body is diploid sporophyte; seedless. Examples: Selaginella, Equisetum (horsetail), ferns like Dryopteris.
Gymnosperms: naked seeds (ovules not enclosed in an ovary). Examples: Pinus, Cycas (living fossil), Ginkgo. Male and female cones are borne on the same or different plants.
Angiosperms: seeds enclosed in fruits; divided into dicots (two cotyledons, reticulate venation) and monocots (one cotyledon, parallel venation). Flowers are the reproductive units.
Life cycles: haplontic (e. Volvox), diplontic (e. Fucus, seed plants), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes, e. Ectocarpus); all show alternation of generations.

questions.q: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?
questions.a: They can live on land, but depend on water for sexual reproduction, since their male gametes are flagellated and swim to the egg. They also need a thin film of water for growth. Like amphibians of the animal world, they need both land and water - hence the title.

questions.q: On what basis are algae primarily classified?
questions.a: On the nature of their photosynthetic pigments, the type of stored food reserve and the flagellation pattern.

questions.q: Mention the group names in which archegonia (the female sex organ) is present.
questions.a: Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Gymnosperms.

questions.q: Cyanobacteria are classified under: (a) Protista (b) Plantae (c) Monera (d) Algae
questions.a: (c) Monera, as they are prokaryotic.

chapters.title: Animal Kingdom
points: Basis of classification: level of organisation, body symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord.
Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms), bilateral (most animals from Platyhelminthes onwards).
Body cavity (coelom): acoelomates (Platyhelminthes), pseudocoelomates (Aschelminthes, e. Ascaris), coelomates (Annelida onwards).
